name: Ganesha
story: Ganesha is honored at the start of new endeavors and is traditionally invoked before important undertakings, journeys, and ceremonies. In most accounts he is the son of Shiva and Parvati. His elephant head is widely understood as a symbol of wisdom and discernment, and devotees regard him as a remover of obstacles on the path toward a goal.
imageAlt: Kalighat painting of four-armed, elephant-headed Ganesha seated on a yellow throne with a halo

name: Shiva
story: Shiva is one of the principal forms through which the divine is understood in many Hindu traditions, associated with transformation, meditation, and the dissolving of what no longer serves growth. He is often depicted in deep meditation on Mount Kailash, and as Nataraja performing the cosmic dance that balances creation and change.
imageAlt: Basohli painting of Shiva and Devi seated on an elephant hide, c. 1675-80

name: Parvati
story: Parvati is honored as a goddess of devotion, strength, and nurturing love, and is traditionally regarded as the consort of Shiva and mother of Ganesha and Kartikeya. Her story of steady, patient devotion is often cited as an example of determination, and she also appears in forms such as Durga and Kali when fierce protection is called for.
imageAlt: Kalighat painting of Parvati placing a wedding garland on Shiva

name: Vishnu
story: Vishnu is understood in many traditions as the preserver who maintains balance (dharma) in the universe. He is said to take on avatars, or earthly forms, in times of great need — Krishna and Rama among the most widely known — in order to restore harmony. He is often depicted resting on the serpent Shesha, with Lakshmi by his side.
imageAlt: Pahari painting of Vishnu resting on the serpent Ananta, c. 1700

name: Lakshmi
story: Lakshmi is honored as a goddess of prosperity, abundance, and well-being, understood by many devotees in both material and spiritual senses. She is especially celebrated during Diwali, when homes are cleaned and lit with lamps to welcome her presence. She is traditionally regarded as the consort of Vishnu.
imageAlt: Kalighat painting of Lakshmi flanked by elephants (Gajalakshmi)

name: Saraswati
story: Saraswati is honored as a goddess of knowledge, music, and the arts, often invoked by students and artists at the start of study or creative work. She is traditionally depicted seated on a white lotus or swan, playing the veena, symbolizing the harmony between knowledge and creative expression.
imageAlt: Kalighat painting of Lakshmi and Saraswati, each standing on a lotus, Saraswati holding a stringed instrument

name: Krishna
story: Krishna is regarded in many traditions as an avatar of Vishnu, known for his childhood stories in Vrindavan as well as his teachings as an adult, most famously the guidance he gives in the Bhagavad Gita. He is often depicted playing the flute, and devotees relate to him through both his playful nature and his role as a spiritual guide.
imageAlt: Kalighat painting of blue-skinned Krishna ferrying Radha across the Yamuna River

name: Rama
story: Rama is honored as an avatar of Vishnu and the central figure of the Ramayana, an epic that follows his commitment to duty and righteous conduct (dharma) even through exile and hardship. His return to Ayodhya after defeating Ravana is commemorated by many as part of the celebration of Diwali.
imageAlt: Kalighat painting of Rama and Sita enthroned with Lakshmana and Hanuman attending

name: Hanuman
story: Hanuman is celebrated for his unwavering devotion to Rama and for the courage and strength he showed in the Ramayana, including his journey to Lanka in search of Sita. He is widely regarded as an example of selfless service and loyalty, and many devotees recite hymns in his honor for strength and protection.
imageAlt: Kalighat painting of Hanuman carrying Rama and Lakshmana on his shoulders

name: Durga
story: Durga is a fierce and protective form of the goddess, called upon when courage is needed to face adversity. According to tradition she was created from the combined energies of several deities to defeat the buffalo demon Mahishasura, and she is celebrated widely during Navratri and Durga Puja as a symbol of the triumph of good over evil.
imageAlt: Kalighat painting of ten-armed Durga defeating the buffalo demon Mahisha

name: Kali
story: Kali is a powerful and often misunderstood form of the goddess, associated with the destruction of ego, illusion, and fear rather than destruction in a literal or negative sense. Her fierce imagery is understood within Hindu tradition as representing the clearing away of what obstructs spiritual liberation. Interpretations of Kali vary across regions and lineages, and she is approached with deep reverence rather than fear by her devotees.
imageAlt: Kalighat painting of the goddess Kali with a sword, third eye and garland

name: Kartikeya
story: Kartikeya, also known as Murugan, Skanda, or Subramanya in different regions, is honored as the son of Shiva and Parvati and is associated with courage, discipline, and victory over negative forces. He is especially revered in South Indian and Tamil traditions, where Thaipusam is celebrated as one of his major festivals.
imageAlt: 19th-century painting of Kartikeya standing in front of a peacock

name: Radha
story: Radha is honored as the beloved companion of Krishna and is seen by many devotees as the embodiment of pure, devoted love for the divine. Their relationship is often interpreted symbolically, representing the soul's longing for union with the divine, and Radha is held in especially high regard within devotional (bhakti) traditions centered on Krishna.

name: Sita
story: Sita is honored for her integrity and resilience throughout the trials recounted in the Ramayana, including her exile and captivity. She is traditionally regarded as an incarnation of the goddess Lakshmi and the consort of Rama, and her steadfastness is frequently discussed as a central theme of the epic.
imageAlt: Illustration of Sita with Rama and Lakshmana

name: Brahma
story: Brahma is traditionally regarded as the creator within the Trimurti, the three principal divine functions alongside Vishnu (preservation) and Shiva (transformation). He is often depicted with four heads, representing the four Vedas, and is associated with knowledge and the creative force behind the universe. Compared to Vishnu and Shiva, Brahma is worshipped at relatively few dedicated temples today, though he remains an important figure in Hindu cosmology.
imageAlt: Kalighat painting of four-headed, four-armed Brahma with his swan mount
